evidence_quotes.quote: To address this need, we used an exploratory case study approach, interviewing employees from seven CBS organizations and gathering documentation, to identify the perceived drivers and strategies employed to mitigate attrition.

They have achieved a single-payer system, through which the organization partners with a municipality on service provision. The municipality appears to maintain service across users regardless of household ability to pay.

Therefore, when households cannot afford their subscription fees, and no other sanitation subsidies are available, cases described having to make the tough decision to remove subscribers from the service completely or otherwise risk becoming ﬁnancially unsustainable.

While Case C, E, and F may experience more ﬁnancial security by forging a customer base that is more likely to pay consistently and fully, pursuing this strategy leaves them less likely to service the poorest households in their service area.
This type of attrition was described by three cases (A, E, F), all of which responded by adopting a minimum 1-year subscription period to subscribe to their CBS services.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to safely managed container-based sanitation (CBS) subscription services, focusing on subscriber retention, service termination, and exclusion.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain reading: examines institutional, governance, and administrative arrangements of sanitation providers along the public-private continuum (ownership, funding, mode of social control, and municipal single-payer partnerships). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing sanitation service access and exclusion, including eligibility screening ('customer vetting' based on ability to pay), tariff/cost-recovery rules and service removal for arrears, administrative discretion/accommodation (individualized one-on-one repayment arrangements vs. strict payment policy enforcement), contractual rules (1-year minimum subscription commitments and early-termination exit fees), and public-private provider/municipal single-payer institutional structures governing universal vs. ability-to-pay access.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical exploratory comparative case study of seven established CBS organizations (operating >=3 years), drawing on semi-structured interviews with administrative representatives, organizational documents and subscriber/attrition data, collaborative qualitative coding, and participant member checking.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to sanitation service access, continuity/retention, affordability, and exclusion: organization-level customer attrition rates (0% under municipal single-payer Case B vs. 0.34% to 3% annually or 1.2%/month across other cases), disconnection/removal for inability to pay, payment compliance differentials under vetting, and exclusion of the poorest and transient households from safely managed sanitation.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (organization-level comparative case study of seven CBS service providers serving 46 to 4,203 subscriber accounts or one municipality of 80,000 individuals across urban and rural contexts; specific countries anonymized for confidentiality), exposure (public-private institutional models and administrative/contractual attrition-mitigation rules), outcome (subscriber attrition, service retention, affordability, and exclusion), and study design (exploratory multi-case qualitative case study) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Exploratory comparative multi-case qualitative study (semi-structured interviews, document review, and member checking across seven organizations)
country: not reported (seven anonymized organizations across multiple countries and continents)
population_and_sample: Seven established container-based sanitation (CBS) organizations (operating >=3 years; 6 urban, 1 rural; serving 46 to 4,203 subscriber accounts and 1 municipality of 80,000 individuals), assessed via semi-structured interviews with 1 administrative representative per organization (n = 7 organizations) and organizational documentation
exposure: Institutional financing/governance positioning along the public-private continuum (municipal single-payer partnership vs. external subsidies vs. internal cost-recovery) and administrative/contractual rules governing service access (customer vetting/eligibility screening by ability to pay, individualized repayment accommodations vs. disconnection for non-payment, 1-year minimum subscription contracts, and early-termination exit fees)
outcome: Subscriber attrition/retention rates, service removal due to inability to pay, affordability barriers, and exclusion of economically vulnerable and transient households from safely managed CBS sanitation services
rationale: Full-text empirical comparative case study examining how container-based sanitation (CBS) providers' institutional models (municipal single-payer vs. subsidized non-profit vs. internal cost-recovery social enterprise) and concrete rule-type mechanisms—eligibility screening ('customer vetting' on ability to pay), disconnection for non-payment, discretionary one-on-one repayment accommodations, 1-year minimum contract commitments, and early-termination exit fees—govern household sanitation service retention, affordability, and exclusion of low-income and transient households. Meets all inclusion criteria (c1–c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2; qualitative/case-study empirical evidence is eligible for systematic review synthesis regardless of quantitative pooling.
